title: TD And BMO Among 9 Banks Accused Of Discriminating Against Conservative Customers, US Regulator Says
desc:
TD And BMO Among 9 Banks Accused Of Discriminating Against Conservative Customers, US Regulator Says

Authored by Jennifer Cowan via The Epoch Times,

A U.S. banking regulator's report has flagged the Bank of Montreal and TD Bank alongside seven other financial institutions accused of restricting financial services to certain American customers because of their conservative political or religious beliefs.

The U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has published a report based on its findings during a supervisory review of debanking practices across nine major banks under its jurisdiction, based on 100,000 complaints at institutions it regulates. Debanking is when a bank or financial institution suddenly closes a customer's bank accounts or refuses to provide financial services.

Joining the two largest Canadian banks on the OCC's list were JPMorgan Chase & Co. - the world's largest banking institution - plus Bank of America Corp., Citigroup Inc., Wells Fargo & Co., U.S. Bancorp, Capital One Financial Corp., and PNC Financial Services Group Inc.

The OCC says its review stemmed from a presidential directive issued by Donald Trump last August which mandated that U.S. citizens cannot be excluded from accessing financial services based on their religious convictions or political viewpoints.

Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould says the banks named in the report "denied, debanked, and discriminated against customers and lawful businesses" between 2020 and 2025.

"Americans should have access to financial services regardless of their beliefs, affiliations, or political views," Gould said in a press release. "Fair access to financial services is not a mantra - it is a mandate. The Trump Administration is committed to ending the weaponization of finance against hardworking Americans, once and for all."

TD did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report, while BMO directed The Epoch Times to a previously issued statement from the Bank Policy Institute.

"We support efforts to establish clear and consistent standards that promote access while maintaining sound risk management, including the administration's recent efforts to prioritize supervisory attention on material financial risk and rather than reputational risk," the statement said.

"We look forward to continued engagement with the administration and Congress as they consider additional proposals that ensure that political or religious beliefs do not unfairly affect customers' access to banking services."

The regulator's report presents examples from the financial institutions of practices it deemed to be an issue. Here's a look at some of the complaints.

TD

TD was listed in the report several times, notably for its management of accounts belonging to an organization dedicated to advancing pro-life advocacy and a faith-based health care sharing ministry.

The OCC reported that the bank instituted a policy requiring that loan requests from the pro-life non-profit organization be flagged for review by TD's reputational risk committee.

The organization's national director was also identified by the bank as having a "high political and media profile," the report found.

TD's line of credit to the faith-based health ministry was determined by the bank to carry a "reputation risk," if the relationship became public knowledge through media coverage or advocacy groups critical of the group's operations.

The bank determined that the group's "moral and religious requirements" to access services conflicted with "TD's values of diversity and inclusion."

BMO

The report highlighted BMO's approach to firearms-related businesses, noting that in 2022 the bank assessed the "reputational risks" of lending to a longstanding customer that manufactured empty firearm magazines and other tactical products.

"The customer was part of a family of companies that had a 'strong relationship' with the bank dating back several decades," the report said.

BMO's environmental and social risk policy directed account managers to understand their customers' businesses and work with those whose practices did not meet the bank's firearms and ammunition guidelines to bring them into compliance before the next credit decision. If existing customers refused to meet the requirements, managers were expected to work toward ending the banking relationship.

A senior risk officer ultimately approved maintaining the relationship but required ongoing monitoring. The bank also established a quarterly threshold requiring tactical products to account for less than 30 percent of the customer's total sales.

Other Findings

The report listed several examples of payment processor WePay, which is owned by JPMorgan, closing customer accounts because of their political or religious views.

One of these instances occurred in February 2021, when WePay closed the account of a merchant that sold merchandise promoting Trump's Make America Great Again (MAGA) brand.

It also closed accounts later that year of a merchant that sold "conservative/ republican" t-shirts and hats, as well as that of a customer that it deemed to be a "religious conservative non profit with strong anti LGBTQ rhetoric."

Another merchant saw its account shut down after handling transactions for an upcoming event, prompted by social media commentary from the event's organizer that described then-President Joe Biden and Dr. Anthony Fauci as enemies and characterized Black Lives Matter activists as Marxists.

JPMorgan Chase said in a statement that it has since "improved the way we do business" and prohibits discrimination against customers based on political or religious views.

The OCC did not announce any bank penalties in its report, but it signalled that it is currently reviewing additional regulatory and supervisory measures to avert similar occurrences in the future.

The U.S. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau responded to the report in a press release this week by promising to address any "harm" caused by the debanking.

It said it would "fully investigate whether the institutions featured in OCC's report and others have complied with federal consumer financial laws and take appropriate action."

title: Judge Orders Trump Admin To Reopen 2027 Diversity Visa Lottery
desc:
Judge Orders Trump Admin To Reopen 2027 Diversity Visa Lottery

Authored by Kimberly Hayek via The Epoch Times,

A federal judge on Wednesday ordered Secretary of State Marco Rubio to open registration for the 2027 Diversity Immigrant Visa Program by Nov. 1.

The ruling by U.S. District Judge Jinsook Ohta of the Southern District of California requires the State Department to announce the registration period no later than midnight ET Oct. 29, open a 30-day electronic entry window by midnight Nov. 1, and notify selectees by midnight Dec. 3.

The department must accept entries and process applications until the fiscal year 2027 visa allocation runs out, or Sept. 30, 2027, whichever comes first.

The program was suspended days after a Dec. 13 shooting at Brown University, which killed two students and injured nine. Officials said the suspect was granted entry to the United States under the program.

"This heinous individual should never have been allowed in our country," then Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said at the time. "At President Trump's direction, I am immediately directing [U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services] to pause the DV1 program to ensure no more Americans are harmed by this disastrous program."

Red Eagle Law, a California immigration firm, initially sued Rubio on Aug. 19, arguing the State Department's failure to open the 2027 lottery was a violation of federal law.

The firm requested emergency relief to restart the program. Judge Ohta denied a temporary restraining order on Sept. 3, citing problems with timing.

She later heard arguments on a preliminary injunction, and then set an oral ruling for Oct. 14. The government had contended that statutory deadlines for running the program had already passed.

The Diversity Immigrant Visa Program was created by the Immigration Act of 1990. It allows nationals of certain countries with low rates of immigration to be granted lawful permanent residency (LPR) after an annual lottery.

The program allows for up to 55,000 individuals to receive LPR status after entering an annual lottery conducted by the State Department. The winning lots are apportioned across six regions of the world.

To apply, candidates are required only to have either a high school education or two years of work experience in a job that requires two years of training. Registration usually opens in early October and closes in early November.

The program was frozen during the pandemic, but in September 2020 a federal judge ordered the first Trump administration to resume it.

"There is no statutory requirement that every available diversity visa be issued each year," U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta wrote in his ruling. "But that does not mean that the State Department could effectively extinguish the diversity program for a given year by simply sitting on its hands and letting all pending diversity visa applications time out."

Trump has long sought to scrap the diversity visa lottery, saying it brings "the worst of the worst" into the country.

In a separate case, a federal judge in August struck down a Trump administration policy that suspended immigrant visa issuance for applicants from 75 countries.

"Consular officers were ordered to refuse immigrant visas to nationals of the 75 designated countries, regardless of whether the consular officer had, following an individualized assessment, determined that the applicant was not likely to become a public charge and that the applicant was otherwise eligible for a visa," U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas wrote.

Lululemon Restructures Fabric Team After See-Through Leggings Complaints And Stock Collapse

Lululemon is restructuring its fabric development operations following another round of customer complaints about product quality, eliminating seven positions and shifting some responsibilities closer to overseas suppliers, according to Bloomberg.

The changes, implemented in August, include moving certain raw-material development functions to vendor partners. The company is currently advertising related positions in Taipei and Ho Chi Minh City.

Bloomberg writes that the shakeup follows complaints that leggings from Lululemon’s Get Low collection were too transparent, prompting a temporary suspension of online sales. Similar concerns emerged weeks later over its heart-patterned leggings.

The problems add to a history of quality-control issues. In 2024, Lululemon discontinued its Breezethrough leggings following criticism of their fit, while in 2013, the company recalled nearly 20% of its women’s bottoms over excessive sheerness.

It comes during an already disastrous year for Lululemon shareholders. The stock has plunged roughly 55% in 2026, dramatically underperforming the broader market as investors question whether the once-dominant athleticwear brand can regain its footing.

The company's financial performance has done little to restore confidence. Second-quarter revenue declined 4% to $2.4 billion, while comparable sales fell 9%, including a 12% decline in the Americas. Management has repeatedly lowered its outlook and now expects full-year revenue to decline between 5% and 7%, a remarkable reversal for a company once celebrated for its consistent growth.

Competition has also intensified, with emerging brands like Alo Yoga and Vuori challenging Lululemon's dominance in premium athleticwear. Meanwhile, merchandising missteps, declining customer traffic and concerns about product quality have raised questions about whether the company's once-formidable pricing power and brand loyalty are beginning to erode.

Shares are now trading more than 80% below their late-2023 peak, leaving new CEO Heidi O'Neill with a difficult turnaround ahead.

While the stock's collapse has made its valuation considerably cheaper, investors appear increasingly unwilling to pay a premium for a company struggling with declining sales, intensifying competition and repeated product failures. For now, the question is whether Lululemon is simply experiencing a temporary rough patch or confronting a more permanent deterioration in its brand.

title: Anthropic To Feed Claude Official Voting Data Ahead Of November Midterms
desc:
Anthropic To Feed Claude Official Voting Data Ahead Of November Midterms

Authored by Kimberly Hayek via The Epoch Times,

Anthropic announced Wednesday that it will add official U.S. voting information and election results supplied by the nonprofit Democracy Works to its Claude chatbot ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Democracy Works provides "Americans with the guidance they need to vote in every election, every time." The nonprofit first partnered with Anthropic in 2024 "to prevent the misuse of AI in political contexts." In April 2026, Anthropic began showing Democracy Works' nonpartisan TurboVote tool in a banner when Claude was asked about voting registration, locations, or dates.

Later this month, Claude will start drawing official voting information from Democracy Works into its responses on Claude.ai for users in the United States, Anthropic said.

"Someone asking where to vote or what ID to bring to their polling place will now get an answer specific to their state, without leaving the conversation," the company said. "These responses draw on publicly available information that Democracy Works collects from state and local election sources."

Claude will also begin showing up-to-date results on election night and in the days that follow.

"When people ask for current vote counts or election results, they'll be shown the latest official numbers directly in their conversation," Anthropic said. "Our goal is for Claude to be a useful tool for political conversations, while preventing election-related abuse."

Conversations that touch on politics, public policy, or social issues make up about 5.75 percent of all U.S. chats on Claude.ai, Anthropic reported after reviewing 250,000 conversations from late September. About 0.51 percent focused on elections or voting. Requests for advice on whom or what to support appeared in just 0.01 percent of those exchanges. Policy violations were rarer still, at roughly 0.002 percent. Most requests stay informational, Anthropic said, with people asking where candidates stand on issues, weighing policy arguments, or drafting documents.

The company expects political queries to climb as Election Day nears.

"More people are turning to Claude for information about this year's elections than ever before," Anthropic said. "We have a responsibility to make sure the answers they get are accurate and balanced, and that Claude isn't used to undermine the democratic process."

Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 scored 99 percent on the firm's political evenhandedness evaluation - the highest to date.

"When people ask Claude about politics, they should get accurate and evenhanded answers that don't favor any particular political viewpoint," the company said.

Independent reviews by the Future of Free Speech, the Foundation for American Innovation, and the Collective Intelligence Project found the models rarely refuse political requests but sometimes insert unsolicited caveats.

Anthropic added new detection tools that look for harmful activity spread across several steps, such as building fake news sites or running schemes that appear ordinary when examined one piece at a time. Tests by the Institute for Strategic Dialogue and the McCain Institute found that Claude stops single, clearly harmful requests but can miss coordinated efforts broken into smaller, harmless-looking tasks.

"Building on these findings and our own, we've added new classifiers to better identify novel and multi-step misuse," Anthropic said.

AI-powered chatbots and search engines are increasingly used to find and summarize election information online, but they are not official sources and frequently cite incorrect information. Anthropic said it will keep testing for political evenhandedness and misuse as the cycle intensifies.

"We'll continue to invest in making Claude more evenhanded, preventing and addressing misuse, and being transparent in our actions," the company said. "This work will be critical in the upcoming U.S. midterms and extends to elections around the world as well."

Anthropic has faced separate scrutiny this year over model access, export controls, and government contracts, though those disputes sit outside its voting information plan.

title: Cocoa Grindings Crush Estimates, Chocolate Stocks Rise: Is Hershey A Buy?
desc:
Cocoa Grindings Crush Estimates, Chocolate Stocks Rise: Is Hershey A Buy?

A new Bloomberg survey found that third-quarter cocoa processing in Asia and Europe exceeded estimates, signaling a potential demand recovery as lower bean costs improve processing margins. The rebound follows a period of record-high cocoa prices that sparked demand destruction among consumers.

Asian processing soared 29% in the third quarter to its highest quarterly level since 2011, according to the Cocoa Association of Asia. In Europe, grindings rose 3.2% from one year ago, marking the region's first quarterly year-on-year increase since 2024, according to the European Cocoa Association.

New York cocoa futures rose .5% on Thursday to about $5,762 a ton, roughly 157% above this year's low of $2,243. Despite the rebound, prices remain more than 50% below the $12,000 levels reached at the height of the cocoa shortage in late 2024

"The market was already trending in a bullish direction and this will add to the sentiment," said Daryl Kryst, senior vice president of OTC commodities at StoneX, adding that weather and supply risks in West Africa linger.

Chocolate stocks have also rallied over the past five days, led by Nestlé and Barry Callebaut, up 6.62% and 6.60%, respectively. Mondelez gained 5.71%, Lindt rose 5.38%, and Hershey added 3.61%.

"Some chocolate companies have been saying that they intend to rebuild volume sales and to focus on volume sales growth," said Rabobank analyst Oran van Dort. "And if that's the case, then this increase in European grindings could be an element of that in preparation."

Lower bean prices this year have improved margins and encouraged activity after the 2024 price spike forced chocolate makers to change recipes and consumers revolted against expensive candy bars. Still, CoBank economist Billy Roberts pointed out that the rebound partly reflects weak comparisons following earlier declines.

Processing strength has yet to translate into a sustained recovery in chocolate demand. A key test will be the "October/Halloween" period, which Deutsche Bank consumer staples analyst Steve Powers highlighted as an important demand signal for Hershey.

"September consumption and share trends were softer than expected, raising the importance of October/Halloween performance in assessing both near-term holiday prospects and the credibility of HSY's expected volume/share improvement into FY27," Powers wrote in a note on Wednseday.

title: AVs Drive More Safely... But Can Lead Nearby Human Drivers To Take Risks: Study
desc:
AVs Drive More Safely... But Can Lead Nearby Human Drivers To Take Risks: Study

Authored by Jeremy Lott via The Epoch Times,

The way automated vehicles (AVs) drive frustrates many motorists sharing the road with them, leading to more dangerous driving and possibly road rage.

That is one way to interpret the findings of researchers at Chinese universities in a newly released paper that aims to gauge the effects of integrating AVs into car fleets worldwide.

"Automated vehicles drive safer but induce riskier behavior in human drivers in car-following scenarios" is the title of the new paper, published in the journal Communications Engineering in October.

Researchers Yueying Chu and Peng Liu from Zhejiang University, and Ying Gao and Zhigang Xu from Chang'an University, sought to answer two questions using available AV driving data: Will AVs drive more safely? And will AVs make nearby human drivers drive safer?

The answer to the first question was yes.

"Our evidence clearly shows that AVs drive safer and smoother as compared to their human counterparts in car-following," the researchers reported.

The answer to the second question was complicated, and potentially deadly.

Cars following AVs tend to drive more slowly because that is what drivers most often do when a slow car is in front of them. In that sense, the behavior of human-driven vehicles was coded as safer.

The reason AVs tend to be the slower cars is that they are programmed to obey all traffic laws and treat speed limits as an upper bound, not a suggestion.

Yet following behind AVs also led human drivers to engage in behavior that the researchers coded as risky. Human-driven cars followed AVs more closely, which is another way of saying they tailgated them.

The Chinese researchers examined several reasons why this might be the case. Their best answer was that because AVs in the lead do not tend to vary their speed, human drivers are more comfortable leaving a smaller gap.

"So, ironically, AVs' better velocity and acceleration management might, unconsciously or implicitly, lead their human followers to maintain a shorter distance and create higher tailgating potentials," they write.

The paper did not examine passing.

On a road with multiple lanes in both directions, passing is relatively safe behavior. Statistically, on two-lane roads, it is much more dangerous because it can lead to collisions with oncoming traffic, sideswipes, or other damaging, often fatal, outcomes.

More tailgating wasn't the only potentially dangerous finding in the paper. It also found that because AVs tend to leave more distance than humans would between themselves and the lead car, other human-driven cars are more likely to "cut in" to that gap, which can lead to accidents, the Chinese researchers found.

That AVs leave significant room and that humans tend to tailgate them is consistent with other findings involving AVs and accidents.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called safety "critical" to the success of the AV industry.

Duffy wrote in an introduction to a September report that AVs "don't drive drunk, they don't get tired, and they can't get distracted by an incoming text message or notification - all significant contributors to crashes today."

The Department of Transportation said it is preparing for "both human-driven and automated vehicles coexisting on public roads" for the foreseeable future.

The safety record of AVs is usually better than that of human drivers, studies have shown.

A July study released by the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety found that the L4 class of Waymo's AV taxis crash at "police-reportable" rates that are 68 percent lower than those of comparable human drivers traveling the same roads under the same conditions.

"Waymo's rate of rear-ending another vehicle was 91 percent lower; its vehicles' rate of being rear-ended was 40 percent lower," the study found.

title: The Blue Wave Trade: JPMorgan's "Democrat Factor" Soars 20% As Wall Street Prices A Sweep
desc:
The Blue Wave Trade: JPMorgan's "Democrat Factor" Soars 20% As Wall Street Prices A Sweep

Prediction markets aren't the only place where traders are betting on a Democratic sweep.

Over the weekend, we laid out Goldman's case that gas prices are steering the midterms, with Polymarket pricing a roughly 65% chance that Democrats take both chambers, a number the bank's own historical work suggests is too high.

But for those who prefer their political bets with a ticker and a prime broker attached, there is another, far more lucrative gauge of how Wall Street sees November 3: JPMorgan's Democrat Factor (JP9DEMP Index on Bloomberg), a beta-neutral long/short equity pair built to move with the Democrats' odds, and nothing else.

It has done exactly that. Since August, the pair is up roughly 20%. Over the same period the S&P 500 rose 2.6%. Scaled up to a 6% volatility target, JPMorgan's Delta-One desk calculates that the Democrat Factor has generated ~170% annualized, a return that would make even the most die-hard AI longs green with envy (although lately that would be red).

In other words, the blue wave is already a trade, and a crowded one at that.

Read on as we explain what is inside JPMorgan's election factor, why it has been tracking Polymarket tick for tick, and why the S&P 500, which is sitting just shy of record highs, has priced almost none of the outcome that BofA's Michael Hartnett says would send it 10% lower.

What Is The "Democrat Factor"?

The construction was laid out by JPM's Delta-One strategist Manish Sinha in the bank's "US Election Series - Midterms: September 30, 2026" note (available to pro subs). The idea predates this election: JPM first built the framework during the 2024 presidential race, and dusted it off for the midterms. The process, as JPM describes it, is to score a universe of roughly 3,000 US stocks by how each reacts to changes in Polymarket's odds, assign each one an "Election Score" for its sensitivity to Democratic versus Republican chances, then optimize the results into two liquid long/short pairs:

The Republican pair (JP9REPP) and Democratic pair (JP9DEMP) are designed to be beta-neutral, aiming to capture election-related idiosyncratic movements. The model also allows us to evaluate a portfolio's direct exposure to Democratic versus Republican factors ahead of the midterm election. This provides a framework to hedge anticipated election uncertainty and to reduce overall risk and directional exposure.

The Democratic pair goes long JP9DEML and shorts JP9DEMS; the Republican pair is the mirror image (long JP9REPL, short JP9REPS). Here is how the two looked at the end of September, overlaid on Polymarket's Senate odds for each party: the Dem factor up 19.45% as Democratic Senate odds jumped above 60%, the Republican factor down 14.57% as GOP odds collapsed.

The more important point is what the factor doesn't contain. JPM's attribution shows that the move is almost entirely idiosyncratic, i.e., stock-specific, with "limited explanatory power from traditional risk factors." The green "Factors" line in the chart below has barely moved since March; virtually all of the August-September surge comes from the red "Idiosyncratic" line.

Translation: this is a pure election bet, unaffected by the AI trade, by momentum, by rates and by beta, and that is precisely why the desk has been pitching it to institutional investors in size.

Tracking Polymarket Tick For Tick

On October 7, with markets digesting what JPM called non-consensus risks in Res Vol and Momentum, Sinha flagged one factor that had held up no matter what:

Regardless of shifting conditions, our Democratic factor (JP9DEMP Index) has continued to show strength as we move closer to the mid-terms. It's up ~20% since August, and that move appears broadly neutral to Beta, Momentum, and other factors.

TRADE – A tactical long in (JP9DEMP Index) could add alpha into the election—especially if Polymarket's continues to trend in Democrats' favor.

The chart that accompanied the note shows why: since the summer the factor (black, right axis) and Polymarket's Democratic Senate odds (orange, left axis, last at 65%) have been nearly indistinguishable, with the factor up 21.9% from its July trough.

A day later, in a JPM S&T factor risk note, that recommended buying protection into year-end and earnings given a negative equity risk premium, Sinha slotted "Long Democrat Pair JP9DEMP" right next to his hedges, noting it "has been tracking Polymarket odds" and "could be a tactical election trade if Polymarket odds keep moving toward Democrats." By this morning's JPM Market Intel briefing the pitch had become a scoreboard: a 6-vol Democrat Factor strategy has generated ~170% annualized returns since August, compared to ~15% annualized for the ~15%-vol S&P, which Sinha says "suggests a meaningful shift in where alpha is being realized, likely driven by election dynamics."

Some napkin math: both numbers describe the same ~20% move. 20% in roughly ten weeks annualizes to the high-100s, and the 6-vol scaling just puts it on the same risk footing as the index. Impressive, but nobody should read it as an eight-bagger in four trading days.

Which brings us to the obvious problem with a factor whose only input is a probability.

From 23% To 64%... And Possibly Back To 58%

The Democrat Factor has worked because the odds have moved, and they have moved a lot. In August, just 23% of fund managers in BofA's FMS expected a Democratic sweep; 47% expected the "GOP Senate & DEM House" split. By Sep 4, Kalshi had a sweep at 47% (as we noted in "Democrat Sweep? Here Are JPMorgan's Midterm Trades - And Why Gridlock Pays"), and three days later we flagged that Polymarket's odds had hit a record:

Odds of a Dem midterm sweep hit all time high 52% https://t.co/O7Iv4Va96b

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) September 7, 2026

By Sep 29, Goldman's average of Kalshi and Polymarket hit ~65% on Oct 8, and in his latest "Midterms, Bidterms, Skidterms" Flow Show (available for pro subs), Hartnett had Polymarket at 64% for a sweep, up from 49% in September, against 28% for the GOP Senate/Dem House split and just 9% for a GOP sweep:

Put the snapshots side by side and the shift is stark: a sweep went from a 1-in-4 fringe call among fund managers to the market's base case in under two months.

The last bar is where it gets interesting for anyone long the factor. As we detailed yesterday, in the bank's "US Election Monitor: October 8 Update" (also available to pro subs) Goldman's Alec Phillips found that in past midterms (2002, 2006, 2010, 2018, 2022), prediction markets "have tended to overstate the challenging party's sweep odds at this point in the cycle", with the average fade from early October to Election Day about 5 points:

Apply the average fade to Goldman's 63% (exhibit above) and a sweep drops to the high 50s. Still the favorite, but if JP9DEMP keeps tracking Polymarket the way it has, a 5-point slide in the odds is a meaningful drawdown for what is now a 20% winner, and potentially a winning arb.

And the risk is lopsided. The odds can't go above 100%, while the polls behind the Senate math are anything but solid. Goldman notes that midterm polls "tend to understate Democrats in Democratic-leaning states and Republicans in Republican-leaning states", consistent with red-state voters "coming home" late, and the Senate majority runs right through Alaska, Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas. Meanwhile, CNN's Harry Enten found that Republicans hold their best party registration position in a midterm year in at least 20 years in Arizona, Nevada, North Carolina and Pennsylvania, a metric he called "pretty gosh darn good" for the GOP.

Put differently, the trade that worked because the odds went from coin flip to base case now needs the odds to go from base case to lock.

What Exactly Is Wall Street Long?

JPM doesn't publish the constituents of JP9DEML and JP9DEMS. But the bank's Delta 1 thematic team (Kaitlyn Bowman and Priyanka Thapa) does spell out what a Democratic Congress would mean at the policy level in its scenario basket JPMDC26P, which we first discussed in early September: long ACA exchange-exposed managed care and hospitals (enhanced premium tax credits get extended) and low-end consumer spending (affordability support); short SMID-cap defense, capital-markets-exposed names (oversight and investigations replace deregulation), energy permitting beneficiaries and anything riding on the CLARITY Act.

That last short has already had a dress rehearsal. When the Senate killed the crypto market-structure bill in mid-September, every Democrat voted no, and we made the obvious extrapolation:

Senators voted 49-50 to reject the so-called Clarity Act Every Democrat voted against the measure. Three Republicans - Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Jerry Moran of Kansas - also voted against the measure. If Dems sweep, data centers are next.

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) September 15, 2026

Hartnett makes the same point with a broader brush: a Democratic sweep "signals electoral shift from populist capitalism to populist socialism" and means "next big direction in tax & regulation up not down (EPS negative)." His preferred hedge, as we first reported on Sep 5, is short financials and the US dollar, which overlaps neatly with JPM's short capital markets leg.

Gridlock Is Good... Unless It's A Sweep

So the election trade is crowded in prediction markets and in the factor space. What about the index? Here the sell-side splits into two camps.

Camp one says relax. JPM's Andrew Tyler argues that even a Blue Wave would fall well short of the two-thirds majorities needed to override a presidential veto, so the result would be gridlock "similar to Biden's last 2 years, Trump 1.0's last 2 years, and Obama's last 2 years", which markets "typically react favorably to."

His conclusion: "Any dip creating around the election, we would be buyers" and history is on his side. Per JPM, the S&P has rallied on average 5.4%, 11.4%, 12.5% and 14.7% at 3, 6, 9 and 12 months after midterm election days since 1990, and all 19 midterms since 1950 showed positive returns 6, 9 and 12 months out.

Goldman's IBD team calls the midterms a potential "clearing event", noting that stocks have historically underperformed into the vote (a median 3.5% decline in the month before since 1974) and outperformed after (a median 6.5% gain over the following four months). Tony Pasquariello made the same point back in August with Ben Snider's analog: 12 of the last 13 midterms saw the market higher from Election Day through the end of February.

Camp two says the base case is the bear case. Hartnett's scenario map: a Democratic sweep is "big risk-off", with "stocks skid >10%", the dollar and yields falling into year-end and international stocks outperforming. A GOP Senate/Dem House split is risk-on (stocks +5%, "Gridlock = Goldilocks"), and a GOP sweep would be the most bullish surprise of all. Goldman's custom basket head Louis Miller is in the same camp, warning earlier this month that "midterms beckon and the result probably won't be risk positive."

Note the problem: the average historical outcome bakes in plenty of gridlock, while the outcome now priced at roughly two-in-three is precisely the one Hartnett says breaks the pattern. In August, when the FMS expected the split, the two camps agreed. Now they don't, because the market's base case has moved from Hartnett's "risk-on" scenario to his "risk-off" one.

And yet the index hasn't blinked. US stocks are up 13.4% YTD per Hartnett's scoreboard, and JPM's own chart shows the S&P up just 2.6% since August while the Democrat Factor ripped 20%. The election risk has been isolated, packaged into a beta-neutral pair, and traded as alpha, and the rest of the tape (held up, as Miller put it, by the AI trade) has been left to assume gridlock.

Bottom Line

Sinha's summary of the trade is hard to argue with:

Where is the market's alpha headed into the midterm? A 6-vol Democrat Factor (JP9DEMP Index) pure-alpha strategy has generated ~170% annualized returns since August. ... This suggests a meaningful shift in where alpha is being realized, likely driven by election dynamics.

Our take is less enthusiastic. The Democrat Factor has been a spectacular way to monetize the odds moving from a coin flip to the base case, but with Polymarket at 64%, Goldman's history pointing to a ~5-point fade, red-state polls that have historically flattered Democrats, and a gas price that could break either way (Trump has already ruled out striking Iran before Nov 3), the easy money in the factor has been made. The bigger mispricing sits on the other side of the ledger: an index that has priced a sweep in prediction markets and in a pair trade, but not in the S&P itself.

If Hartnett is right that a sweep means a 10% skid, the cheapest election hedge on the board is downside protection on an index that still trades as if the split is the base case. Then again, with 22 days to go, it may be that the only thing the market truly believes in is gridlock = goldilocks... and gas below $4.

title: X Suspends 13,000 Accounts In Suspected China-Russia-Iran Operations Targeting US Politics
desc:
X Suspends 13,000 Accounts In Suspected China-Russia-Iran Operations Targeting US Politics

Authored by Arthur Zhang via The Epoch Times,

Social media platform X has suspended more than 13,000 accounts involved in three suspected foreign influence operations linked to China, Russia, and Iran that targeted American political discussions ahead of the November midterm elections.

In an Oct. 14 announcement, X said the networks used fake accounts to publish and amplify political content targeting U.S. candidates and public figures across the political spectrum.

The company identified the accounts through proactive monitoring and investigations by its Safety team.

X did not disclose how many accounts were associated with each country, identify the American candidates targeted, or publicly release evidence linking the networks to specific foreign government agencies.

The suspensions come less than three weeks before the Nov. 3 elections, when Americans will elect all 435 voting members of the House of Representatives, approximately one-third of the Senate, and numerous state and local officials.

Election Safeguards

X said its election-related enforcement builds on safety measures operating year-round, particularly its rules against coordinated inauthentic behavior, which prohibit organized efforts to manipulate discussions through deceptive accounts.

"Whether it is spam networks or entities engaged in influence operations, we are actively working to identify and stop coordinated inauthentic behavior that undermines the integrity of our platform," the company said.

Under its Civic Integrity Policy, X also addresses misleading information about when, where, and how people can vote, along with deceptive efforts to discourage electoral participation.

The platform said users can report suspected civic integrity violations through a process that routes submissions to Community Notes, which allow contributors to add context to posts.

X may also apply labels to posts in serious cases.

The announcement comes as the Justice Department has stepped up election-integrity prosecutions.

On Oct. 12, the department announced charges involving 16 individuals in cases concerning illegal voting, fraudulent voter registration, and related offenses. The allegations are not related to the suspected online influence operations disclosed by X.

In response to an Epoch Times' inquiry about suspected foreign influence operations and election-integrity enforcement, a Justice Department spokesperson said on Oct. 15 that the department would not confirm or deny whether it was conducting an investigation.

"The department remains committed to keeping America's elections in the hands of Americans and without foreign influence, and will use every available tool to deter, disrupt, and hold accountable those who violate federal law," the spokesperson said.

Earlier Chinese Influence Operations

X previously disclosed in August that it had identified approximately 200,000 suspected Chinese bot accounts, including about 200 posting content that could manipulate American debates over AI data centers and energy policy.

Such operations have also involved accounts posing as Americans.

In September 2024, Microsoft reported that Chinese Communist Party-linked influence operators impersonated U.S. voters, asked Americans about divisive political issues, and engaged with users across the political spectrum.

Chinese researchers have separately explored how American political opinions could be influenced.

In a December 2024 paper, researchers at the Communication University of China described using artificial intelligence to create 101 simulated American voters and expose them to segments of a 2020 presidential debate between Donald Trump and Joe Biden.

The virtual voters discussed the candidates' statements, reconsidered their positions, and cast ballots over six rounds.

The researchers tracked how support for the candidates shifted as the simulated voters exchanged information and revised their preferences.

The research was a computer simulation, not a documented attempt to influence actual voters.

No public connection has been established between that research, the earlier influence operations, and X's latest suspensions.

desc:
Trump Directs DOJ To Seek Capital Punishment For Killers Of Police, Firefighters

Authored by Jill McLaughlin via The Epoch Times,

President Donald Trump told first responders on Oct. 15 that he was pushing the Department of Justice (DOJ) to seek capital punishment for murderers convicted of killing members of law enforcement or firefighters.

"We're bringing the death penalty back for anybody that kills a police officer, by the way, or anybody in law enforcement," Trump said at a White House Rose Garden luncheon honoring America's law enforcement and firefighters.

He said he directed the DOJ to pursue capital punishment for people convicted of killing a police officer, but also asked the department to add the punishment for anyone who murders a firefighter.

"They're on the ladder and they get shot at and nobody ever talks about that," Trump said. "You'll see - shootings will stop very quickly."

"America owes our first responders a debt it can never fully repay," he said. "But as president, I will always stand behind those who stand on the front lines of law enforcement, fighting fires, all of the things that you people do so courageously."

National Border Patrol Council President Paul Perez told the president that first responders have "never had the support or leadership from any administration that we have from you."

"And it's because of you that America is stronger, America is safer, and the border is totally secure because of you and your leadership," Perez said.

National Volunteer Fire Council Chairman Steve Hirsch presented the president with a fire helmet at the luncheon.

"While this helmet protects us in a fire or a wreck, we want it to protect you," Hirsch said. "We want God to wrap his protective arm around you and use this helmet - remember that we want you to be protected by our Lord."

The U.S. Fire Administration reported that 30 on-duty firefighters have been shot and killed by gunfire in the United States since 1990.

An average of about 50 officers are killed intentionally every year by firearms or other weapons, according to FBI statistics.

The federal government and U.S. military still allow death penalty sentencing, along with 27 states, while 23 states, as well as Washington, D.C., have abolished it.

Four states - California, Pennsylvania, Oregon, and Ohio - allow capital punishment but have placed an executive hold on death penalty cases.

Many U.S. states still consider murdering a law enforcement officer a capital offense with added circumstances. But in the four states that have a hold on executions, the death penalty cannot be applied.

Yesterday’s retail sales suggest that energy prices may be eroding some consumer demand. Headline sales rose 0.8% on the month, but much of that increase was due to petrol sales – or, rather, prices. Excluding autos and gas, underlying sales printed a weaker-than-expected 0.1% m/m increase.

But more importantly, perhaps, are the recent wobbles in the AI trade. Rising rates were already complicating the funding required for the sector’s huge investment plans. And investors are perhaps getting apprehensive about the large sums that AI-related companies are asking for. Concerns about competition from China added to that mix this week, after CXMT claimed it has made a breakthrough in memory chip technology.

So, AI-related stocks have had a tough few days, CoreWeave’s bonds made headlines for not exactly the best reasons, and the FT writes that investor are “dumping data centre bonds” more broadly. With so much of economic growth currently riding on the AI boom, those wobbles were probably the main reason for the fall in Treasury yields: a flight to safety, and perhaps revised estimates of how strong demand and therefore growth and inflationary pressures will be going forward.

Despite these growing pains, Fed Chair Warsh remains an AI believer. At the IMF’s annual meeting, the Fed Chair repeated that investments in artificial intelligence are a huge benefit to the US economy. Even if the path is will be “very bumpy,” it will ultimately be “very good” for wealth in the US and other countries that adopt AI. This optimism, and the lack of any hints that the Fed may need to hike rates again in October, provide some support for equities today.

AI investors are not the only ones worried about Chinese competition. Trade data released this week suggest that China’s exports to Europe have risen sharply. That particularly relates to cars and AI-related electronics. The EU reached an agreement with China last week that would limit the export of hybrid cars into the bloc, and the European Commission may take further steps to protect its own industry.

Bloomberg reports that Brussels is scrutinizing trade data to detect surges in imports. That would be a first step towards new import quotas on goods being shipped from China or other countries. Bloomberg’s source notes that the EU will probably use the agreement it reached with China on hybrid vehicles as a blueprint for other sectors – which means that any new quota on sectors or goods would be set at a high-enough level to limit the risk of retaliation. Having said that, Beijing has already warned the EU against “new tricks” with respect to its trade policy.

The news fits with our conclusion that structural forces are pushing the EU and China towards greater confrontation on trade, as China’s economic reliance on exports clashes with Europe’s determination to protect strategic industries. However, as my colleagues note in their report, both China and the EU possess significant leverage in their bilateral trade relationship, even as their power rests on different foundations and operates over different time horizons. We therefore believe that a US-style conflict is less likely than a managed escalation that includes negotiations, de-risking, and selective retaliation.

The final estimate of the Eurozone HICP statistics confirmed that headline inflation ran at 3.8% in September, and that core inflation continues to run at 2.5% – keeping the ECB on track for additional tightening, but probably not until December.

The ECB’s Wunsh confirmed that the recent rise in longer-dated yields does not necessarily prevent some further rate hikes. The rise in long-term yields has tightened financial conditions, but Wunsh argues that it has had limited effect on Eurozone financing, which is shorter-term. While wage developments remain “benign,” the policymaker argues that the ECB cannot wait for visible second-round effects before acting.

Indeed, that would mean the central bank has fallen behind the curve, and policymakers will be wary of making a similar mistake as the previous energy shock. Yet, acting more forcefully before such evidence materializes would meaningfully increase the risk that the ECB errs on the side of too tight monetary policy.

title: Mamdani Moves To Ban Horse Carriages From NYC, Drivers React
desc:
Mamdani Moves To Ban Horse Carriages From NYC, Drivers React

Authored by Nicholas Zifcak via The Epoch Times,

Mayor Zohran Mamdani has confirmed that he and the City Council speaker have agreed to phase out carriage horse rides in Central Park, a win for animal rights activists who have long opposed the rides.

The mayor said he would make sure workers and owners are protected as the rides wind down, with an end date of June 1, 2028.

"I think that we have a civic responsibility to ensure that we are not leaving anybody out to dry," Mamdani said at an unrelated press conference Oct. 14. The City Council announced it will vote on the bill ending carriage rides on Oct. 22.

The Transport Workers Union, which represents the carriage drivers, denounced the text of the bill as noncommittal, with "no meaningful economic relief for workers." The bill does not require the city to compensate the 68 owners for their city-issued license or medallion.

Mamdani said the city's plan will become more explicit and options are still being discussed. The mayor said he would make sure owners and workers won't be made to pay "for the sunsetting of an industry."

However, drivers say they feel they have been treated poorly, and that the City Council has no solid justification for the ban.

In a statement, the union denounced City Council Speaker Julie Menin for what it described as using "the tragic death of a tourist to contrive a public safety crisis."

On June 17, Romanch Mahajan, 18, a tourist visiting from India, was thrown from a carriage after the horse spooked and bolted during a ride with his family. Mahajan hit his head and died. After his death, Menin announced her support for the ban in a video on X.

Carriage horse drivers argue the issue is not public safety. Mahajan's death is the first in more than 160 years of horse-drawn carriages operating under the union in Central Park, compared to as many as 28 deaths related to bikes, e-bikes, and scooters on New York streets in 2026 alone. Menin and Mamdani have yet to set new safety measures on e-bikes and scooters.

Animal rights groups have long sought to end the carriage horses in Central Park, launching social media campaigns whenever there is a horse-related incident, such as the death of a carriage horse named Deniz on June 9 after he ate Japanese yew growing in the park.

Animal rights group New Yorkers for Clean, Livable, and Safe Streets (NYCLASS) reacted on X to the ban.

"For decades, NYCLASS fought to end cruel and dangerous horse carriages," it wrote. "It took the extraordinary courage, compassion, and unwavering leadership of Speaker Menin."

Drivers say that the horses are well-treated and that extensive city rules govern their feeding schedule, what time of day they can work, as well as the temperature range during which horses are not allowed to work (18 degrees or colder, 90 degrees or warmer). The city also mandates an eight-hour workday and five weeks of vacation time for the horses every year.

'No Way!'

Carriage license owner Ahmet Bilici, who trained as a veterinarian in Turkey before coming to the United States in 2001, became a carriage driver to support himself as he was learning English. The job stuck, and he's been a driver for 23 years. He said that if the City Council wanted to work with carriage drivers, drivers would be amenable, but that City Council just wants a ban.

"When you take this carriage from me, I am going to lose my quarter century! No way!" he said. "I trusted the city because the city licensed the medallion, and now you are shutting down? No way!"

Bilici said the ban will hurt 300 families if you count support staff, which includes stable workers, blacksmiths producing horseshoes, and craftsmen making saddles.

"This is my small business, my investment. It's like my house. You're burning my house!"

Bilici said that if the city shuts down the carriage rides, it must compensate drivers.

"There's no way we can accept this," he said.

Another driver, Danielle Slot, also said she was extremely disappointed. She thinks there is no solid justification for the ban.

"Our City Council is supposed to look out for people and represent people, and they're supposed to see through these things," said Slot, referring to the long-term campaign of NYCLASS head Steven Nislick to ban carriage horses, which dates to 2008.

Slot previously worked with horse-drawn carriages on Michigan's Mackinac Island, a 4-square-mile island in Lake Huron that never welcomed automobiles and still relies on horse-drawn carriages.

"I've just completely lost faith in the government here, which is very sad," said Slot. "It feels like they're capitalizing on sensationalism."

Slot said she voted for Mamdani.

She said City Council members are unaware of the realities of the equine industry, thinking as if a new home can easily be found for horses where they won't need to work. The proposed ban requires owners to make sure horses are not sold off to other carriage drivers out of state.

"It's a really nice thought that there would be some magical sanctuary. But it's just not realistic," said Slot, who added that caring for horses costs thousands of dollars a year. She said those on the City Council supporting the bill either don't know, or they don't care.

Slot moved to New York to work as an actor and is still pursuing her career in the performing arts. She said she came to New York in part "because this is a place where I feel like people are protected, people can be who they want to be," but she said her experience with the ban on horse-drawn carriages makes her feel the political system is compromised.

title: Bad Inflation Cures Itself. Good Inflation Doesn't
desc:
Bad Inflation Cures Itself. Good Inflation Doesn't

Authored by Lance Roberts via RealInvestmentAdvice.com,

Key Takeaways

  • Inflation driven by supply shocks is "bad" inflation, and bad inflation is self-liquidating because rising income doesn't support it.
  • September headline CPI ran 3.7% while core sat at 2.6%. The gap is gasoline, up 34.2% over the year and now more than half of the monthly increase.
  • Real wages have turned negative, and labor's share of output just set its lowest reading since the series began in 1947.
  • The 10-year breakeven sits near 2.3%. The market that gets paid to price inflation is not pricing an inflation problem.

Most of the argument about inflation right now is a fight between people using the same word for two completely different things. One side sees a 3.7% headline print and starts sketching a repeat of 1979. The other sees core running more than a point below it and declares the problem solved. Both are reading the same release. The distinction that matters is not how big the number is, but whether anybody's income is financing it. That is the line between "good" inflation and bad inflation, and almost nobody draws it.

Good Inflation, Bad Inflation, And The Difference Nobody Makes

There is a general framework to inflation, and it is older than any of us. Prices can rise because buyers are bidding for scarce goods with money they've actually earned. Or prices can rise because the cost of producing something has jumped for reasons unrelated to demand. An oil embargo will do it, as we saw in the 1970s. So does a shuttered Strait of Hormuz, a new tariff schedule, or a pandemic that takes half the world's shipping capacity offline for eighteen months.

This is an important point for the "debasement" crowd, whose narrative overlooks the underlying fundamentals.

"The following economic illustration is taught in every 'Econ 101' class. Unsurprisingly, inflation is the consequence if supply is restricted and demand increases via monetary interventions."

However, there is a very important distinction to be made about inflation. The first type is the "good" kind of inflation, and it is genuinely good. Demand pushes prices up; firms book wider margins; tight labor markets funnel those margins into paychecks, and the higher paychecks fund the higher prices. The loop closes and becomes self-reinforcing because every leg of it is paid for by real output.

The second kind, the "bad" kind of inflation, closes nothing. A tariff is a tax, just like an oil shock is a tax. Somebody's cost went up, and the money has to come out of a budget that did not grow. Every dollar of that price increase is a dollar not spent somewhere else. Bad inflation doesn't create the income that pays for it, so it destroys the demand that supports it. Such is the mechanism behind the oldest saying in commodities: "high prices cure high prices."

Think of it this way. A group of people drives the same way to work every day. Half get a raise, the other half doesn't. The city decides to put a toll booth on the road they drive to work; each year, that toll rises. Both groups have an increasing number draining their bank accounts each month. However, only one group has sufficient compensation to continue using the toll road. The group without the compensation raise is eventually forced to stop using the toll road; traffic falls, and the operator cuts the toll to win them back.

What The September Print Actually Says

Let's review the recent August data to see what the message, versus the narrative, actually is. The headline CPI came in at 3.7% year over year in September. Core came in at 2.6%, a tick higher than August. Read that pair again, because it is the whole argument. The gap between them widened from nine-tenths of a point to one and a tenth, meaning the headline accelerated roughly three times faster than the core.

That gap suggests a very different narrative than what the media suggests. Gasoline rose 9.1% in the month alone and 34.2% over the year, and the BLS attributes over half the entire monthly increase in the all-items index to that one category. Energy overall is up 20.4%. Meanwhile, core goods, where a genuine demand boom would show up first and loudest, rose 0.7% over twelve months, sitting exactly where it was in August. Shelter ticked up to 3.2%

Now the part I owe you, because I set a test in advance. Core ticked up, shelter ticked up, and services' less energy reached 3.1%, which would eventually prove me wrong. One month of tenths is noise rather than a trend. It is also the first month this year that those three moved the wrong way together, and core goods holding flat at 0.7% is why I am not moving yet, because that is where a demand boom announces itself first, and it has not.

Headline CPI pulled further away from core in September. The shaded area is the spread, and the spread is energy. Source: BLS via Massive Market Data, September 2026.

I've been making this argument since June, when I wrote about why the May 4.2% headline was an oil story rather than a demand story. To wit:

"A 4.2% headline that is three-fifths gasoline is not the same animal as a 4.2% headline driven by wages, rents, and services broadening."

Four months later, the composition has not changed. What has changed is that the evidence against the demand-pull story got considerably stronger.

Labor Just Set A 79-Year Low

The most important evidence comes from the labor market. If this were the "good" kind of inflation, workers would be capturing some of it. They are not.

Real average hourly earnings fell 0.7% over the twelve months through September, more than double the August decline. Nominal wages rose 0.1% on the month against a 0.6% CPI print, so purchasing power went backward at the fastest pace of the year. Run the same calculation off average hourly earnings and CPI, and you land in the same place. Real wage growth is near -0.7%, down from over 1.5% as recently as last spring.

In April 2026, real wage growth crossed below zero and hit its weakest reading in September. The gold bars represent the months when wages grew faster than prices. The red bars are months when they didn't. Source: BLS via Massive Market Data, August 2026.

Then there is the one number that everyone simply overlooked. In the second quarter, labor's share of nonfarm business output fell to 52.8%. The Bureau of Labor Statistics flagged that as the lowest level in a series that begins in the first quarter of 1947. Read that again. There have been 79 years of data, 2 dozen business cycles, 4 major wars, the Volcker shock, the China trade shock, and the pandemic. Despite all that, in what is supposed to be an economic boom, we just set a record low.

Labor's share of nonfarm business output in Q2 2026, the lowest reading since the series began in 1947.

Labor's share of output has been falling for a quarter century and just made a series low. Good inflation requires this line to rise. Source: BLS, Productivity and Costs, Q2 2026.

Stop and notice that in the chart above, this is not a 2026 event. The erosion in labor runs back to the early 2000s, long before "artificial intelligence" or "surging debt." The last two years have simply accelerated the numbers. With respect to the inflation question, the timing matters most. A price level that is rising while labor's slice of output hits an all-time low is the textbook signature of cost pass-through rather than demand-pull. In this environment, corporations are fixated on protecting profit margins, while workers are absorbing the difference.

The economic activity surveys tell the same story if you take the time to read past the headlines. The ISM services printed 54.9 in September, with new orders easing to 59.8. That reads like a demand boom until you see prices paid at 74.0, the highest since July 2022, against an employment index that has not managed to exceed 50.1 in three months. Steady orders, hot input costs, flat payrolls. When respondents were asked what was driving those costs, fuel came up about twice as often as anything else.

Where The Inflation Bulls Have A Point

As always, we need to examine both sides of every argument, as the inflation bulls do have a valid point.

The strongest one is the AI buildout. Memory is genuinely scarce; its scarcity is genuinely caused by capital spending, and the producer price index for storage devices has climbed 23% since the end of 2024, while import prices for computers and parts are up 37%. J.P. Morgan's research team puts the memory shock at 0.2% to 0.4% on core inflation. That is capex-driven price pressure; it is real, and it did not come from an embargo. However, that scarcity will eventually reverse. As with oil prices, high prices eventually curtail demand.

The second argument is that tariffs are a policy choice, not a weather event. That is a true statement, and a tariff regime that stays in place for years produces a price level that stays elevated for years. Calling that "transitory" is a semantic trick. I can't argue with that. A permanent tax produces a permanent price. However, the current tariffs were not enacted by Congressional legislation, which would make them more permanent. In this case, they were enacted through executive order, which means the next Administration can repeal them quickly.

The third is that energy is not reliably mean-reverting on any schedule you can trade. Geopolitics doesn't run on a calendar. However, high oil prices, as shown in the chart below, reliably mean-revert over time.

Those are all sound and valid arguments, but there is a problem with all three, though. Every one of them describes a SUPPLY constraint. A memory shortage is, by definition, a shortage. Call the tariff what it is: a tax. And the Middle East risk is a supply risk. None of them creates the income that pays the higher price. All three fail the same test: gasoline fails, and a more flattering story doesn't change what the bill does to a household budget.

Why Bad Inflation Cures Itself

"Inflation is inflation. My grocery bill doesn't care about the taxonomy."

That is a fair statement. The pain from inflation is the same either way, and when you are staring at the number on the gas pump, the squeeze on household budgets happens regardless. Just because it happens to be the academically preferable kind, the household budget just doesn't care. However, the taxonomy isn't about how it feels, but how it ends, and bad inflation ends in a way the good kind never does.

Every major energy spike since 1971 has reversed within one to two years. The 2008 spike gave way to a 25% collapse. The 2022 spike gave way to a 17% collapse. Source: BLS, CPI energy index via FRED, through September 2026.

Notably, look at what happens after every spike on that chart. In June 2008, energy jumped by more than 24%, then subsequently fell by 25% over the following year. In June 2022, energy surged by 41.5%, then only to fall by 16.6% by 2023. Every period from the 1974 and 1980 shocks, the 2000 run, and the 2015 collapse is the same. The pattern repeats itself because it has to, since "demand destruction" is not an economic theory; it's just arithmetic. The current reading of roughly 20% sits well inside the range that has always reverted.

Such is why the bond market refuses to panic. The 10-year breakeven inflation rate is 2.33% as of October 13, and the September monthly average was 2.36%. That number has barely moved all year, holding a range of roughly 2.24% to 2.44% while headline CPI swung from 2.4% up to 4.2% and back to 3.7%. The one market that gets paid to be right about inflation looked at an 180-basis-point headline swing and didn't blink. It then watched September print three-tenths hotter and tick down.

Critically, this is where the case from the "Persistent Purveyors Of Doom" gets confused with itself. Yes, bond yields are elevated, and the bears point at that as vindication for their case. The 10-year sits near 5.1% and the 30-year above 5.55%. But if you decompose it, the rise is due to real yield and the term premium, not inflation expectations, because expectations have been pinned near 2.3% for 18 months. Since early September, the long bond has added about 30 basis points, while the breakeven has given up 3. The bears are right that the long end is repricing. They just have the wrong reason.

Five tests, and five answers pointing in the same direction, which all bring to mind a rule to live by.

"When every strategist on television agrees that inflation is structural and yields only go up, the setup is usually pointed the other way."

What This Means For Portfolios

Will bad inflation cure itself on a schedule you can put in a calendar? No. Demand destruction takes quarters, not weeks, and an energy shock can persist long enough to cause real damage as it resolves. Such is the frustration of running a process that works in quarters for clients who measure in weeks. But will it resolve without the Fed having to break something? On this evidence, probably yes, and that is a very different portfolio than the one the inflation-forever crowd is selling.

It argues for duration, which is the position I laid out in my discussion about wage growth as a leading inflation indicator. Since then, the real wage data has reinforced that positioning. Investors who bought commodity-linked exposure as an inflation hedge may have the wrong trade. The reason is that commodities would hedge the one kind of inflation that has historically unwound. However, quality equities with pricing power beat the debt-heavy cyclicals that need a nominal boom to work. Most notably, watch the labor data rather than the CPI headline. Labor is where the answer lives.

In the current environment, as laid out in the "Druckenmiller Warning," an effective bond sleeve would look something like this.

Here is what would change my mind, stated plainly so you can hold me to it. If core services excluding shelter reaccelerate, if the Employment Cost Index turns up, if real hourly earnings cross back above zero, and the quits rate rises, then the wage loop is closing, and this inflation became the durable kind while I was arguing it wasn't. Watch those four. I'd rather be corrected by data than by a client's statement.

The thing to fear was never that prices would keep climbing. It's that they'll stop climbing because nobody can afford them anymore, and labor's share of output has been telling us for twenty-five years exactly which of those two we're heading toward.

title: Federal Judge Tosses Ex-CIA Chief Brennan's 'Speculative' Lawsuit Against Trump Admin
desc:
Federal Judge Tosses Ex-CIA Chief Brennan's 'Speculative' Lawsuit Against Trump Admin

Authored by Debra Heine via American Greatness,

A federal judge on Thursday threw out former CIA Director John Brennan's lawsuit, which sought to compel the Trump administration to preserve records for his defense against potential criminal charges, ruling that he lacked standing.

The Department of Justice is investigating claims that Brennan and other national security officials conspired to undermine President Donald Trump.

The suit, filed in July 2026, sought to compel the Justice Department to retain investigative records so Brennan could prove any indictment against him was the result of vindictive or selective prosecution by the Trump administration.

Judge Jia Cobb, a Clinton-appointed judge, described Brennan's allegations of political targeting as "deeply concerning," but determined the claimed injury was "speculative" and not yet imminent, as no indictment has been filed.

Brennan was President Barack Obama's CIA director from March 2013 to January 2017, and before that, Obama's counterterrorism adviser.

He is facing indictment in at least two investigations: the broader "grand conspiracy" probe into the 2016 election interference inquiry and a separate case regarding alleged false statements made to Congress in 2023.

Prosecutors in the Southern District of Florida are examining allegations that Obama and Biden-era intelligence and law enforcement officials conspired to deprive President Trump of his civil rights through various investigations, from the 2016 Russia probe and the intelligence community assessment to the Mar-a-Lago classified documents case and related matters.

According to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee, Brennan "made numerous willfully and intentionally false statements of material fact" during his testimony in 2023, including:

  • Falsely denying that the CIA relied on the discredited Steele dossier in drafting the post-2016 election Intelligence Community Assessment; and

  • Falsely testifying when he told the Committee that the CIA opposed including the Steele dossier in the Intelligence Community Assessment (ICA).

  • These statements were contradicted by the record established by the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence (HPSCI) and the CIA, the committee stated in a press release in October 2025.

Newly declassified documents show:

  • A CIA officer drafted the annex containing a summary of the dossier;

  • Brennan made the ultimate decision, along with then-FBI Director James Comey, to include information from the dossier in the ICA; and

  • Brennan overruled senior CIA officers who objected to the inclusion of the dossier material.

The former CIA director argued in his lawsuit that because he planned to contest any prosecution that arises from the DOJ's probes as vindictive and selective, internal records and communications would be needed to establish that in court.

Brennan alleged that President Trump had singled him out in retaliation for his role in the Russian collusion hoax.

Cobb appeared to that aspect of Brennan's case seriously, saying that "if he was eventually able to prove those allegations true, that would certainly suggest that his potential prosecution is vindictive."

But at this point, the judge said it remains to be seen that Brennan is facing enough harm to bring the lawsuit.

"Even taking all of Brennan's allegations to be truthful at this stage," the judge wrote, "the injury he alleges is simply too attenuated from the actions he seeks to enjoin to warrant a finding of standing here."

With the Fed about to enter its blackout ahead of the October 27-28 meeting, Warsh declined to push back against rate expectations, saying he doesn’t “prejudge meetings”, despite this week’s hotter inflation numbers. Instead, he was strikingly upbeat about the US economy, talking about a “massive investment surge” and the potentially huge productivity benefits from AI. Markets took the lack of hawkishness as good news, with October hike pricing dropping to around 15% from roughly 30% as he spoke, while S&P and Nasdaq futures are both +0.15% higher having been negative for most of the session before he spoke. Stoxx futures are +0.68% higher.

title: Americans' Trust In Fellow Voters Falls To Fifty Year Low; Survey Finds
desc:
Americans' Trust In Fellow Voters Falls To Fifty Year Low; Survey Finds

Authored by Bryan Hyde via American Greatness,

Americans' trust in their fellow citizens' voting judgment has fallen to its lowest recorded level in more than five decades, according to a recently published Gallup survey.

American voters' growing distrust of political leaders and institutions now extends to one another, with Democrats and Republicans showing similar levels of skepticism.

According to Gallup, 51% of U.S. adults have a great deal or fair amount of trust in Americans as a whole to make democratic judgments - the lowest reading since Gallup began tracking the measure in 1974.

Five measures of trust in the federal government are at low points in Gallup's trends. pic.twitter.com/uwmZXcCJT0

— Gallup (@Gallup) October 14, 2026

Axios reports the distrust cuts across party lines with just 53 percent of Democrats, 51 percent of Republicans and 49 percent of independents trusting Americans' ability to make democratic decisions.

While the public's skepticism was historically aimed at political leaders and government institutions, the growing partisan divide has now caused citizens to lose faith in one another, reflecting a deeper systemic shift.

According to the Pew Research Center, public trust in the electorate's democratic judgment has been on a downward trajectory for several decades, accelerating sharply in recent years.

Trust stood at 86 percent in 1976 and 78 percent in both 2002 and 2005, but has stayed below 60percent since 2018, according to Gallup.

The Gallup survey found that Americans have more trust in their local government (67 percent) and state government (55 percent) than in their fellow citizens' democratic judgment (51 percent), according to Axios.

Democrats are more likely than Republicans and independents to trust both local and state governments.

Gallup reports Republicans still largely retain trust in the federal government, albeit somewhat less than a year ago.

The survey also revealed that 42 percent of Americans say they trust politicians who hold or seek public office, while 33 percent trust the news media.

The erosion of peer-to-peer trust is particularly concerning to political scientists who say the trend poses a unique challenge to democratic norms.

When voters view the opposing side not merely as political rivals but as fundamentally incapable of sound democratic decision-making, it undermines the willingness of the defeated party to accept election outcomes as valid.

Gallup surveyed 1,000 U.S. adults by landline and cellphone Sept. 1-17, 2026 with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points.

title: Beijing Tightens Grip On Solar Exports: Will Trump Play America's Quartz Card?
desc:
Beijing Tightens Grip On Solar Exports: Will Trump Play America's Quartz Card?

Beijing's new restrictions on advanced solar technologies and equipment suggest the Trump-Xi meeting in Washington did little to ease trade tensions. The new measures aim to preserve China's technological advantage as the US and India expand domestic solar manufacturing. This reinforces ongoing concerns about critical materials, where Beijing has placed export controls on tungsten, germanium, gallium, and antimony.

Bloomberg cites a statement released by China's Ministry of Commerce earlier this morning announcing that it would add 12 solar-related technologies and core equipment to its export-control list, citing national security concerns. The changes form part of a broader revision covering 40 technologies, including AI and biopharmaceuticals.

"In recent years, the application of solar technology in sensitive fields such as aerospace, national defense, unmanned equipment, and high-security-level infrastructure has been continuously expanding," the ministry said in the statement.

The statement continued, "The national security risks that may be caused by the export of solar technology have been constantly rising. It is necessary to implement timely and appropriate supervision."

The measures include a ban on exports of production technology for perovskite and solar modules, advanced technologies that offer higher efficiency and potential use in space-based solar power. Restrictions will also apply to certain technologies used to produce polysilicon, a key solar-panel material.

According to BloombergNEF analysts, the new controls could complicate efforts to diversify the global solar supply chain. Manufacturers in the US and India still depend on China for some critical materials, equipment, and technologies.

The question now is how the Trump administration will respond, if it can.

Trump administration trade officials could restrict exports of US high-purity quartz to China through export controls and licensing requirements.

China's solar dominance remains vulnerable to restrictions on US-sourced high-purity quartz, giving Trump potential leverage.

LucccA asks: Why are labor unions in the US still not as well-organized compared to the rest of the world? I know there was a push against them in the past—does that still have an effect today? Also, why are there so many right-leaning unions in the US?

Michael: A lot of reasons. The US has low union density compared to other wealthy nations, currently at 10.0%, and that has been on a precipitous decline for the past few decades for a variety of reasons that include anti-union and union busting campaigns, outdated labor laws where employers often retaliate for union organizing or delay bargaining for years, as we are seeing with Starbucks, where there is no union contract after nearly five years since the first store won its union election in December 2021.Right to work laws in the US also undermine labor unions and starve them of resources. To the extent that there are right leaning labor unions in the US, they typically are law enforcement unions that consistently endorse and back Republican candidates despite the Republican Party in the US opposing collective bargaining. Some unions like the Teamsters have been making efforts to get Republicans to support legislation and in turn receive endorsements from the union, and this has shown up this election cycle with the Teamsters endorsing Republicans like Congressman Max Miller or Kansas Senator Roger Marshall, who are both facing very competitive re-election battles.

Heather: There’s a bunch of ideas floating around on cutting costs for groceries, healthcare and energy bills. A key thing Democrats are promising if they regain power in Congress is to wrestle back authority on trade and repeal Trump’s tariffs, which would lower what it costs compaines to import. If Democrats retake the Senate, expect Elizabeth Warren to become chair of the powerful banking committe, and push forward some curbs on private equity investments.
